message.reasoning:
I'm planning a JUnit 4 test suite for ExtendedProperties, mapping out the branches to cover in interpolate/interpolateHelper, escape, unescape, countPreceding, and endsWithSlash.

Continuing the plan, I'm listing more areas to test: PropertiesReader.readProperty and PropertiesTokenizer.nextToken branches, constructors, include handling, load's encoding and main parsing loop, getProperty/addProperty/addPropertyDirect/addPropertyInternal type branches, setProperty, save's output/header/value handling, combine, clearProperty, getKeys, and subset.

Given the massive scope of this class, covering getString/getProperties/getStringArray/getVector/getList/getBoolean and all the numeric getter variants along with their null/default/type-mismatch branches, plus testBoolean, convertProperties, and put/putAll/remove, I'll aim for broad but practical coverage rather than exhaustive testing of every single branch.

Using a TemporaryFolder rule for load()-related file tests, I'm planning out systematic test methods: constructor and initialization defaults, getInclude/setInclude behavior across null/empty/custom values, addProperty behavior for single values, comma-separated values, escaped commas, duplicate keys converting to list storage, non-string values, and repeated additions building up a list. I'm also covering setProperty overwrites and clearProperty for both existing and nonexistent keys.

Continuing the test plan, I'm covering getKeys with and without prefixes, subset extraction including edge cases like invalid subsets and exact prefix-length matches, and getString behavior across simple values, interpolation, null handling with and without defaults, list values, and a case where a raw non-String/List object stored via put() should trigger a ClassCastException. I'm also adding tests for getProperties (valid and malformed), plus getStringArray variants covering string sources, list sources, and null handling with and without defaults.

I'm mapping out similar coverage for getVector and getList — pulling from lists and strings, handling nulls with and without defaults, and verifying wrong-type errors throw as expected. For getBoolean, I'm working through true/false variants and noticing something notable in the source: an invalid boolean string doesn't throw but actually falls back to false because of how Boolean's string constructor parses unrecognized values, so I want a test that documents this quirky behavior rather than assuming an exception. I'm also planning a test for the missing-key, no-default case.

Given time constraints, I'm prioritizing getInteger for full branch coverage (instance parsing, string parsing, null defaults, wrong type, missing key) while giving getLong, getDouble, getFloat, getByte, and getShort lighter smoke tests since they share the same underlying logic. Then I'll round out coverage with tests for property conversion, put/putAll/remove behavior, and note that the escape/unescape methods are private static, so testing them will require going through public methods indirectly rather than calling them directly.

I'm planning to test escaping and loading behavior indirectly - checking that addProperty round-trips special characters correctly, that save() escapes commas, and that load() handles comments, blank lines, multiline continuations with backslashes, duplicate key concatenation, file includes, and empty values, using a temp folder for actual file-based tests. I also want to exercise the tokenizer's continuation logic by adding properties with trailing backslashes before delimiters to confirm segments get combined properly.

Given the complexity of the escaping rules, I'll keep the test set representative rather than exhaustive, and move on to interpolation - testing that `${key}` references resolve correctly, that undefined variables are left unresolved, and checking how defaults interact with interpolation, which may require reflection to set the private defaults field.

I also need a test confirming that circular variable references (a pointing to b, b pointing back to a) trigger an IllegalStateException rather than looping forever.

For load(), I'll use a temporary folder to create real property files, testing basic key-value parsing with comments, and separately testing multiline value continuation using backslash line breaks.

I'm digging into the exact backslash-counting logic to figure out how the continuation detection determines odd vs even trailing backslashes before the last character.

After stripping just the trailing backslash, the buffer keeps "key = part1 " with the space intact, since trim() only strips whitespace at the true start/end of the line, and the backslash sitting at the very end means that space stays preserved inside.

So the final key/value comes out correctly with the space preserved, giving "part1 part2" as the trimmed value. Now I want to check duplicate key concatenation behavior, expecting that loading a file with the same key twice yields a vector of both values, and I should also test include file support next.

For the include test, I'll set up a main file referencing "other.properties" in the same temp folder, relying on basePath being derived from the main file's directory. I should also verify that load() skips lines with empty values like "key=", and I'll skip testing absolute include paths since cross-platform separator differences make that too fragile.

For simpler load(InputStream) tests I'll just use ByteArrayInputStream directly, reserving TemporaryFolder only for tests that actually need include resolution or file-based constructors, since basePath only matters when handling includes.

Now I'm assembling the full test file with the necessary imports and writing out the test methods.

Writing helper method logic...

This lets me test the "defaults != null" branches across many getter methods. Given the scope, I'll test representative getters like getInteger, getBoolean, and getString fully with the defaults chain, while keeping other getter tests simpler but still covering basic branches.

For each numeric getter (byte, short, integer, long, float, double), I'm planning to test: value already the correct type returns directly, value as a String gets parsed and stored, missing value with no defaults returns the primitive default via the two-arg method, wrong type stored throws a ClassCastException, and getXxx(key) without default throws NoSuchElementException when the key is entirely missing.

Given the effort budget, I'll write full, thorough coverage for getInteger and getBoolean since those are more complex, then abbreviated 2-3 test methods for byte, short, long, float, and double that just hit the main branches, testing NoSuchElement only once overall.

I should also cover getProperty directly, isInitialized after load and after addProperty, and the subset behavior for prefix matching, exact-key prefix, and invalid subsets returning null. I want to add tests for getKeys with a prefix, combine, a basic display call just to exercise the loop without asserting output, and getProperties for a key.

For getProperties with defaults and malformed input throwing IllegalArgumentException, plus convertProperties, put/putAll/remove — I'll skip null-key and null-value tests since Hashtable disallows nulls and would throw NullPointerException, which isn't the behavior I'm targeting. Now I'm assembling the final test skeleton with coverage rationale comments.

I want to test escape/unescape indirectly through addProperty with backslash-escaped values, being careful to trace through how Java string literals translate into the actual backslash characters being unescaped.

Since there's no comma, this goes straight to unescaping. Tracing through the unescape logic on two backslash characters: it finds the pair, deletes the first one, leaving a single backslash, and then the loop bound shrinks so it stops there.

So the final result is just one backslash character. Now I need to double-check how many backslashes to write in actual Java source code to represent two literal backslash characters -- that requires four backslashes in the source since each pair of two source-backslashes escapes to one real backslash.

So one actual backslash needs two typed in source, meaning two actual backslashes need four typed backslash symbols in the Java string literal. I need to double-check the final output carefully to make sure I put exactly the right number of backslash characters when writing the code.

Actually, this seems overly complex — let me switch to testing with a simpler escaped comma case instead, tracing through exactly how Java parses the literal into actual characters to confirm the string value produced.

Since the token ends with a single backslash (even count of preceding backslashes), it's treated as an escaped delimiter, so the buffer appends "a" plus the delimiter, then continues to the next token "b" which doesn't end with a slash, appending it directly to get "a,b" as the final trimmed result.

This confirms the tokenizer correctly merges escaped commas into one token while unescape leaves "a,b" unchanged since there's no double backslash. I'll write two tests: one verifying that an escaped comma in "a\\,b" produces the single string "a,b", and another verifying that an unescaped comma in "x,y" splits into a two-element array.

Since there's no comma, the code takes the plain branch and unescapes the double-backslash into a single backslash, so I'm confirming the expected test assertion should compare against a Java literal with two backslash characters representing that one actual backslash.

Actually, given how error-prone counting backslashes in text can be, I'll sidestep the risky literal entirely and instead build the two-backslash string by concatenating two single-backslash strings, making the test unambiguous rather than relying on tricky escaped literals.

Writing more test cases...

Tracing through carefully: after deleting index 0, buf is now length 2 ("\b"), and the for-loop increments i to 1. Now checking condition i < buf.length()-1, that's 1 < 1, which is false, so the loop terminates and returns "\b" as expected.

Now I want to keep using this explicit concatenation approach for constructing backslash literals to avoid confusion in the test assertions, and next I'm sketching out the save() test with a comma-containing string value and a list value.

For the save test, I trace through how addProperty splits a comma-containing string during insertion — the value "x,y" actually gets tokenized into two separate calls that add "x" then "y" under the same key, and because the second addPropertyInternal call sees an existing String value it converts the key's value into a Vector containing both tokens rather than storing the literal comma-containing string.

That means the escaping logic for a raw comma inside a saved value isn't actually exercised via addProperty. To really test that path I need to bypass the comma-splitting behavior, perhaps using subset() or another entry point that calls the internal direct-add method to store "x,y" verbatim as a single string.

Tracing through the escape function step by step to confirm it inserts a backslash right before the comma, turning "a,b" into "a\,b" -- matching the expected saved output line "k=a\,b".

",b" confirms the escaping matches expectations, so I'll verify save() produces "k=a\,b" using a substring check rather than pinning down exact formatting with blank lines, keeping the test robust. I'll finalize the test file now, prioritizing good branch coverage over exhaustively testing every numeric getter given size constraints.

For the byte/short/long/float/double getters, I'll write one consolidated test per type covering string parsing, wrong-type exceptions, and missing-with-default cases to save time while still hitting key branches. Now I'm writing the final test code.

EasyMock isn't really needed here since there's nothing to mock — I can just use a plain HashMap for the putAll test instead of ExtendedProperties. I'm now drafting the full test class along with a summary table in Thai afterward, carefully verifying expected behavior for tricky methods like getInclude(), checking the default null case returns the static "include" field.

I'm also tracing through setInclude behavior: passing null or empty string sets includePropertyName to empty, which makes getInclude() return null, while passing a real value returns it directly. For load(InputStream), since encoding defaults to null, the code falls through to the ISO8859_1 reader branch, which succeeds under normal JVM conditions, so the UnsupportedEncodingException paths are hard to trigger without special setup.

I'm realizing I can actually test the invalid-encoding branch by passing an arbitrary bad encoding string to load(input, enc) directly, which triggers the exception in the first try block and falls back to the ISO8859_1 reader in the second block — this covers the "enc invalid, falls back" case. The deepest fallback where even ISO8859_1 is unsupported isn't realistically triggerable on a standard JVM, so I'll skip that case. Now I'm looking at the main parsing loop's branch conditions, starting with lines that have no '=' sign or an '=' at position zero, which should be skipped without calling addProperty.

I also need to test lines where the value trims to empty (skipped via continue), and the include-key handling logic: when setInclude(null) is called, the include check becomes inactive so a line like "include=foo.txt" is just added as a normal property instead of being treated as a file include. Then there's the case where the include key matches but the referenced file doesn't exist — this should fail silently, with no property added for that key.

For the absolute-path branch, I want to check the logic where a value starting with the file separator character is treated specially — I'll try setting up an included file at a real absolute path and using that as the include value to see how it's handled.

Since this is Unix-specific behavior (Windows drive letters don't start with a bare separator), I'll guard that test with Assume.assumeTrue checking File.separator equals "/", so it skips safely on Windows.

For the "./" prefix case, I want to verify that an include value like "./other.properties" correctly strips the leading dot-slash and resolves relative to the base path — this should work cross-platform since it uses the actual file separator variable.

Now I'm thinking through how to set up the file listing and include tests using TemporaryFolder, and running into the fact that basePath is a protected field, which means I may need to instantiate ExtendedProperties directly and rely on package-level access from the same test package rather than reflection.

Actually, redundant same-package imports are fine in Java—they're just unnecessary, not an error—so I'll add the import statement anyway to satisfy the requirement without worrying about it causing issues.

Since the test is in the same package, I can set the protected basePath field directly on the ExtendedProperties instance to point at the test folder, then load properties from a byte stream, sidestepping the need for the real constructor-based file resolution logic.

I'll still test the two-arg and three-arg constructors separately using actual temp files, since those need to exercise real file reading, basePath computation from the file's absolute path, and defaultFile chaining behavior.

I also want to directly verify getProperty(key) branching -- null object with null defaults returns null, while null object with a present defaults chain returns the default's raw value (string or list). With the coverage plan solid, I'll move on to writing the actual test code now, keeping it thorough but concise.

I'll need to import TemporaryFolder and Rule from JUnit, plus Assume for conditional skips, and set up a helper that writes string content to a new file using FileWriter, relying on try-with-resources since Java 7+ is assumed.

For testing save(), I'll capture output with a ByteArrayOutputStream and compare the resulting string. I also want to verify that save(null, ...) short-circuits and returns without throwing, and that combine() correctly overwrites duplicate keys while merging in new ones, checking the final key set and values afterward.

I need to test putAll for both a plain Map and an ExtendedProperties source, confirming values transfer correctly and key ordering is preserved when merging from another ExtendedProperties instance. Then for remove() and put(), I'll check that removing returns the old value and clears the key entirely, while put() returns null when no prior value existed.

Testing put() again reveals something subtle: calling put() on an existing key doesn't overwrite since put() internally calls addProperty rather than setProperty, so a second put actually appends the new value into a Vector rather than replacing the string. Still, put() returns the previous scalar value beforehand, matching Hashtable's contract even though the underlying storage becomes a list -- this duplicate-key append behavior is exactly what the addProperty javadoc describes.

I want to verify this progression: first put returns null, second returns "v1" while converting storage to a list, and a third put on the same key appends again, growing the list to three entries -- checking this through getStringArray length. Then I'll confirm convertProperties() correctly imports a plain java.util.Properties object's entries into an ExtendedProperties instance, and move on to testing subset() by adding several dotted keys and checking that filtering by prefix returns just the matching suffixes.

I also want to cover the edge case where a key equals the prefix exactly with no dot, verify subset() on a nonexistent prefix returns null, and confirm getKeys(prefix) filters correctly. I should also check clearProperty behaves safely on a missing key and properly removes an existing one from both the underlying table and the ordered key list, and that calling display() at least runs without throwing for coverage. With all these cases in mind, I'm ready to assemble the final test code.

I still need to verify getBoolean(String key) with no default: it delegates to getBoolean(key, null), and if the resolved value is null it throws NoSuchElementException rather than returning a default -- so a missing key with no defaults chain should directly raise that exception.

For an invalid string value, testBoolean returns null which then gets passed into Boolean's string constructor; since that constructor treats anything not equal to "true" (including null) as false, the result is Boolean.FALSE rather than an exception, confirming my earlier assumption.

I also need to verify that getByte with a bad numeric string throws NumberFormatException via Byte's string constructor, and that getInteger on a completely missing key with no defaults throws NoSuchElementException since the internal null-defaulting path leads to that failure.

I'm noting one more subtlety: the primitive-returning getInteger(key, defaultValue) overload actually delegates internally using a null Integer default rather than the passed-in default, only falling back to the real default value at the very end.

This confirms the pattern -- the wrapped-Boolean overload for getBoolean never actually triggers NoSuchElementException since the default is pre-wrapped before delegation, so it's mostly a sanity check test. I'm settling on the final set of numeric getter tests: correct type already stored, string parsing success, missing key returning default via primitive overload, wrong type causing ClassCastException, and malformed numeric strings causing NumberFormatException.

I also realize the `defaults` field is private, not package-visible, so I can't set it directly even from the same package -- I'll need to use reflection with setAccessible(true) to inject a defaults object into the test fixture, which is a legitimate testing technique rather than guessing at behavior.

I'll reserve the file-based setup specifically for load/constructor/include-file tests where real IO matters, keeping everything else simplified via reflection. Now I'm ready to write out the comprehensive final test class with well-organized, clearly named test methods.
